data.claude_summary: MANTA is a new benchmark designed to test whether large language models maintain consistent animal welfare reasoning under sustained adversarial pressure across multi-turn conversations. Unlike existing single-turn benchmarks, MANTA's 1,088 five-turn dialogues expose two distinct failure modes: models that recognize welfare concerns in isolation but abandon them when pressed (value instability), and models that fail to surface welfare stakes proactively in everyday queries (low moral sensitivity). Testing seven frontier models reveals that four change their performance ranking between turn-one and later rounds, and that a model's ability to recognize a moral issue does not reliably predict whether it will hold that position under pressure. The benchmark also finds that welfare robustness varies by species category, with companion animals receiving more consistent treatment than farmed animals or invertebrates.
data.key_takeaway: An LLM that passes a standard safety check on ethical reasoning may still capitulate when users push back across multiple conversational turns — a gap that benchmark designers and deploying organizations need to account for.

data.centre_angle: This study finds that delegating information seeking to generative AI can degrade learning outcomes, particularly for higher-order cognition, because the conversational interface reduces user agency and narrows knowledge exploration. data.claude_summary: A field experiment assigned participants to use either ChatGPT or Google Search for informal learning over eight days. Those using ChatGPT offloaded information selection to the AI, which reduced their sense of agency and increased meta-cognitive load. The study identifies two distortions: ChatGPT outputs skew toward solution-oriented answers rather than principled knowledge, and the conversational interface narrows users' exploration of the broader knowledge space. On average, ChatGPT users had worse learning outcomes than Google users, with the gap largest for higher-order critical thinking. The findings suggest a structural tension between AI-assisted information seeking and the kind of active cognitive engagement that produces durable learning.
data.key_takeaway: Using ChatGPT for information seeking can produce worse learning outcomes than traditional search, particularly for critical thinking, because the tool's conversational design encourages cognitive offloading rather than active knowledge construction.

data.centre_angle: This study shows that delegating market decisions to a shared algorithmic provider can produce coordinated outcomes that are empirically indistinguishable from cartel behaviour, even when the competing firms have no direct contact. From CAMO's perspective on algorithmic decision-making, the finding raises a structural question that extends well beyond electricity markets: when organisations outsource consequential decisions to the same AI or optimisation layer, standard competitive analysis becomes unreliable. The paper's conduct-test methodology — estimating counterfactual decisions from first principles and comparing them against observed behaviour — offers a template for regulators and managers who need to audit whether a shared algorithm is steering decisions toward individual or collective optima.
data.claude_summary: When competing firms use bidding algorithms supplied by the same third-party provider, their bids synchronise in ways that effectively coordinate market behaviour without explicit collusion. Studying five-minute battery bids in Australia's electricity market, the paper finds that batteries sharing an autobidding provider forgo profitable dispatch during evening peaks to protect the revenues of same-provider rivals. A conduct parameter near one indicates near-perfect coordination. The effect activates only when a provider controls more than roughly 30% of near-margin capacity, and the estimated consumer harm is $5.5 million annualised. Crucially, standard ownership-based concentration measures would miss this entirely, since the batteries belong to different firms.
data.key_takeaway: When rivals share the same algorithmic bidding provider, the algorithm can act as a de facto coordinator — with real consumer costs that ownership-based competition analysis is blind to.

data.centre_angle: This paper derives formal conditions under which AI substitutes for human labor across organizational layers, finding that middle management faces structural — not merely incidental — vulnerability, and that even highly skilled workers lose protection once AI capability crosses a threshold shaped by organizational depth. Together, both lines of work suggest that the workforce risk from AI is not uniform across levels — it is shaped by organizational architecture, cost asymmetries, and incentive design simultaneously.
data.claude_summary: When does AI replace a human worker, and under what organizational conditions? This paper presents a formal model of Human-AI Task Allocation (HAT) in hierarchical organizations, deriving a precise 'substitution principle' based on the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition (costly and slow) and AI capability scaling (cheaper and faster). The model predicts that AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions rather than gradual ones, that middle-management roles face elevated vulnerability, and that highly skilled workers are protected only up to a threshold shaped by organizational depth and risk differentials. The analysis also suggests AI flattens hierarchies and widens managerial spans of control. The paper is a working paper from arXiv and has not yet undergone peer review.
data.key_takeaway: AI replacement in organizations is not random — it concentrates in middle management and follows a predictable structural logic tied to cost asymmetries, organizational depth, and risk, meaning firms can anticipate vulnerability hot-spots rather than react to them.

data.centre_angle: This study deploys a multimodal LLM as a large-scale compliance auditing instrument—evaluating thousands of corporate disclosures against a regulatory standard rather than relying on human reviewers. data.claude_summary: Buildings generate 37% of energy-related CO₂ emissions, and new regulations in New York and the EU now require firms to report carbon intensity per square metre for comparison against science-based decarbonisation pathways. Using BeDA—a multimodal large-language-model auditing tool applied to 2,246 firms over two decades—this study finds that only about one in five built-environment firm reports discloses the required metric. European real-estate firms comply at roughly twice the rate of their US counterparts. Among firms where intensity can be constructed, 39% already exceed the 1.5°C pathway limit. The finding reframes the obstacle to enforceable stranding regulation: it is not a forecasting problem but a measurable, jurisdiction-specific reporting gap that targeted disclosure mandates—monitored by tools like BeDA—could systematically close.
data.key_takeaway: AI can audit corporate climate disclosures at scale, but four out of five building-sector reports still lack the basic metric—carbon intensity per square metre—that stranding regulation requires, making the reporting gap itself the primary policy problem.

data.centre_angle: This study introduces a validated instrument for measuring two distinct forms of LLM dependency—task-oriented reliance and social-psychological reliance—among Spanish-speaking users. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, the more practically urgent finding is that instrumental dependency (using LLMs as a decision-making crutch) is now measurable at the individual level, which opens the door to assessing whether organizational AI adoption is building genuine capability or deepening unhealthy over-reliance. The scale's weak correlation with need for cognition is worth noting: employees who depend most on LLMs are not simply those who prefer not to think hard, suggesting dependency is shaped more by workflow design and perceived tool trustworthiness than by individual cognitive disposition.
data.claude_summary: As large language models become standard tools for task execution and decision-making at work, researchers have developed and validated a Spanish-language psychometric scale to measure psychological dependency on LLMs. The LLM-D12-SP distinguishes two forms of dependency: instrumental (relying on LLMs to perform tasks and inform decisions) and relational (turning to LLMs for companionship and social interaction). Tested on 386 Spanish-speaking participants, the scale showed strong internal consistency and confirmed that both dependency dimensions correlate with internet addiction and perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, but not with need for cognition. This cross-linguistic validation extends prior English and Arabic versions, offering organizations a standardized tool to diagnose how deeply, and in what ways, employees are psychologically anchored to LLM tools.
data.key_takeaway: Organizations now have a cross-linguistically validated tool to distinguish whether employees depend on LLMs as a decision aid or as a social substitute—a meaningful difference for workforce design and AI governance.

data.centre_angle: This study provides unusually clean causal evidence that replacing human interviewers with AI voice agents improves hiring outcomes — not because AI is more empathetic or creative, but because it is more consistent. data.claude_summary: A natural field experiment with 70,000 job applicants tests what happens when AI voice agents replace human recruiters in structured interviews. Applicants randomly assigned to AI interviewers were 12% more likely to receive job offers, and the gains held through job starts and worker retention, with no productivity penalty among those hired. The mechanism appears to be 'adaptive standardization': AI agents conducted more consistent, structured interviews than human recruiters while still responding to individual applicants, producing cleaner, more decision-relevant signals. The authors argue that AI's core advantage in this setting is variance compression — when information collection is distributed across many human workers, individual inconsistency becomes noise, and AI reduces that noise systematically.
data.key_takeaway: AI interviewers outperformed human recruiters in a 70,000-applicant experiment by being more consistent, not more capable — a reminder that variance in how humans execute routine tasks is itself an organizational cost.

data.centre_angle: This study argues that GenAI platform monetization is not simply a pricing problem but a user-psychology problem: the number and sequencing of subscription tiers shapes how users emotionally and cognitively evaluate their options, with real consequences for retention and revenue. data.claude_summary: How should generative AI platforms price their services without driving users away? This study tests whether ad-supported subscription tiers can help GenAI firms like ChatGPT recover rising operational costs while keeping users engaged. Across four experiments with 1,063 participants, the researchers find that adding a single ad-supported tier nudges free users to upgrade but prompts paying subscribers to downgrade. Offering two ad-supported tiers resolves this tension, retaining paid subscribers while still converting free users. Affective and cognitive evaluations mediate these preferences, and time-intrusive advertising — but not visually intrusive ads — is what most damages user experience. The findings draw on compromise-effect and affective-primacy theories to offer practical pricing-tier design guidance for GenAI platform operators.
data.key_takeaway: Offering two ad-supported tiers — rather than one — lets GenAI platforms grow paid subscriptions without cannibalising existing ones, because it defuses the compromise effect that otherwise pulls paying users down.

data.claude_summary: When lawyers and litigants use AI to draft legal documents, courts demand careful human review — but those review obligations are impossible to discharge without evidence on how often AI tools fail, how severely, and how detectably. Analyzing the official record of the New York court system, this paper finds that rules repeatedly call for evidence that does not yet exist (error rates, do-not-use lists) and substitute procedure — training mandates, checklists, uncalibrated review — in its place. The paper proposes a computing research agenda including task taxonomies, shared error metrics, maintained benchmarks, and test harnesses to supply what the justice system currently lacks.

This conceptual paper introduces the 'Cognitive Commons' framework, drawing on commons theory and distributed cognition to argue that individual AI adoption decisions—each rational in isolation—can collectively deplete the shared pool of professional knowledge a field needs to reproduce itself. Early signals from clinical and labor-market data are suggestive but not yet conclusive, and the paper is explicitly conceptual rather than empirical.
data.key_takeaway: AI adoption may be individually rational for every professional and every firm while collectively hollowing out the expertise base that makes professional AI oversight possible at all.

data.claude_summary: Most organizations deploy AI to automate discrete tasks, yet the largest efficiency losses occur not within tasks but between them — in the coordination overhead of handoffs, approvals, and synchronization across teams and systems. This McKinsey article argues that agentic AI, which can act autonomously across multi-step processes, is best positioned to eliminate this 'coordination tax' rather than merely accelerate individual steps. The implication is that workflow redesign, not tool deployment, is the core challenge. Organizations that focus AI investment on inter-task coordination — rather than intra-task speed — are more likely to see measurable throughput gains. The excerpt is brief and the underlying analysis is not peer-reviewed, so specific empirical claims cannot be verified.
data.key_takeaway: The biggest efficiency gains from agentic AI come from eliminating coordination overhead between workflow steps, not from speeding up the steps themselves — so redesigning handoffs matters more than automating tasks.
